newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: China and Guatemala brief U.N. Council president.
newsitem.headline: China and Guatemala brief U.N. Council president.

text.p: Guatemala and China on Thursday briefed the president of the U.N. Security Council on their talks to rescue a U.N. peacekeeping mission, which Beijing vetoed because of Guatemala's ties to Taiwan.

Council President Hisashi Owada of Japan, who did not give any details, said he did not expect a breakthrough this week on the talks. But one diplomat close to the talks said "there was hope for movement."

The 14 other Security Council members last Friday all supported sending 155 military observers to Guatemala for three months to monitor the U.N.-brokered peace agreements that ended more than three decades of civil war.
But a negative vote by China, one of five permanent council members with veto power, killed the mission.

U.N. spokesman Fred Eckhard said one option was to "go back to the Security Council" on whether or not to approve the peacekeepers. U.N. ambassadors from both countries met on Wednesday but canceled their scheduled talks for Thursday because of a "technical" reason, Owada said.

Diplomats said that China was not asking for an immediate break in relations between Guatemala and Taiwan as a condition for supporting the peacekeepers. But among its demands were that Guatemala stop supporting moves to put U.N. membership for Taiwan on the General Assembly's agenda, they said.
China also has objected to Guatemala's invitation to Taiwan's foreign minister, John Chang, to attend the peace signing ceremonies on Dec. 29 in Guatemala City.
Taipei was expelled from the United Nations in 1971 and replaced by Beijing as the rightful representative of China.

It has given generous economic aid to a host of small nations in Central America, the Caribbean, Africa and in the Pacific, who in turn support getting some kind of recognition for Taiwan at the United Nations.

Should the issue not be resolved in the coming week in the Security Council, diplomats said Mexico and others have threatened to ask the 185-member General Assembly to approve the mission. The assembly has already established a nearly 500-strong human rights monitoring mission in Guatemala, which has a few military officers in its ranks.
But neither China nor the United States welcome this move. China would probably lose the vote and the United States does not want the assembly to override Security Council actions.
In Beijing on Thursday, Foreign Ministry spokesman Shen Guofang said that "the attitude and position of the Chinese government is very flexible on this matter."
"We hope the Guatemala government will take concrete actions to get rid of the obstruction and guarantee they will never support Taiwan either inside or outside the U.N."
Taipei, meanwhile, denounced Beijing for using its Security Council seat to squeeze Latin American states.

"We should altogether condemn communist China's acts of using its influence in the U.N. Security Council to interfere in the internal affairs of Central and South American countries," said a foreign ministry spokesman, Chen Yung-tso.

And in Guatemala City, a presidential spokesman, Ricardo de la Torre, said: "We have been friends with Taiwan since the island has existed as an independent country. Guatemala's position on Taiwan will be maintained. It will not vary."
